deep.reconstruction:
The page is one leaf of Gauss's handwritten table of periodic decimal fractions for prime denominators. It continues the previous page (primes 331–367) and leads to the next (443–463). No derivation is written out. Each block is labelled by a prime p and lists every distinct decimal period of fractions a/p, grouped in tens of digits. If 10 has order e mod p, there are (p−1)/e periods, one for each coset of the subgroup ⟨10⟩ in (Z/p)^*. The period of the coset ⟨10⟩ is always written as the expansion of 10/p (=0.0…); the dotted leading 0 shows this. The other cosets are written as the periods of other numerators.

(1) p=373, e=186=(p−1)/2, so 2 periods.
- Lines 1–2: period of 74/373 = 0.1983914209 1152815013 … 9302949061 662 (186 digits). 74 is a quadratic non-residue: (2/373)=−1 and (37/373)=+1. Since 10 is a residue, ⟨10⟩ is the residue class and this period covers the non-residues.
- Lines 3–5: period of 10/373 = 0.0268096514 … 3672922252 0107238605 8981233243 9678284182 305630 (186 digits).

(2) p=379, e=378: 10 is a primitive root, so one period, that of 10/379 = 0.0263852242 … 6992084432 71767810 (378 digits).

(3) p=383, e=382: 10 is a non-residue ((2/383)=+1, (5/383)=−1), so one period, that of 10/383 = 0.0261096605 … 8877284595 30 (382 digits).

(4) p=389, e=388: one period, that of 10/389 = 0.0257069408 … 7249357326 47814910 (388 digits).

(5) p=397, e=99, 4 periods of 99 digits each:
- 139/397 = 0.3501259445 … 602015113
- 225/397 = 0.5667506297 2292191435 … 5088161209 068010075
- 150/397 = 0.3778337531 … 6725440806 045340050
- 10/397 = 0.0251889168 … 6448362720 403022670
Note 139·100 ≡ 5 (mod 397), so the first period lies in the coset of 5.

(6) p=401, e=200, 2 periods:
- 296/401 = 0.7381546134 … 1296758104 (non-residue coset)
- 10/401 = 0.0249376558 … 0274314214 4638403990

The circled bottom figure (2316) is a digit-count check: 372+378+382+388+396+400 = 2316. The same holds on the neighbouring pages: 2436 = sum of p−1 for 331…367, and 2268 for 443…463.

Use: this is the table described in Disquisitiones Arithmeticae art. 312–318. With it, any fraction a/p is turned into a decimal by finding a's coset and its offset (via indices / the remainder sequence) and reading off the stored period from the right place. Why these particular representative numerators (74, 139, 225, 150, 296) were chosen is not evident from this page (my remark).
errors: p=373, first period, line 2: the true digits after 9865951742 are 6273458445040 followed by 2144772117…. Gauss's interlinear '458' repairs an omission. As transcribed, the group (6273[458]5940) still does not quite match; probably a reading problem, possibly a residual slip.

p=397, last period: the final 9 digits must be 403022670 (397·403022670 ≡ −10 mod 10^9). The pencilled repetition '303022670' (possibly an archivist's restoration where the paper is torn) has the wrong first digit.

p=397, second period: the first line's grouping is irregular (a struck prefix, then '…6297 72292?914 …'), but the digit string agrees with 225/397. In the p=383 block a struck group is followed by '950391 6449086161 8798' — irregular grouping, correct digits.
Apart from these, the blocks checked are correct: their opening digits, closing digits and digit counts all agree with the true periods.

results.what: Complete decimal periods of a/p for p = 373, 379, 383, 389, 397, 401, one period per coset of ⟨10⟩ in (Z/p)^*. Period lengths: 186, 378, 382, 388, 99, 200.
results.modern_name: Table of periods of decimal fractions (reciprocals of primes); multiplicative order of 10 mod p
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Disquisitiones Arithmeticae §§312–318; full table to 1000 published from the Nachlass in Werke II, 1863). Also earlier and later tabulators: Lambert, Burckhardt, Reuschle, Cunningham.

results.what: Arrangement of periods by cosets of the subgroup generated by 10 (quadratic-residue classes when e=(p−1)/2), with a per-page digit-count check equal to the sum of (p−1).

deep.surprise_reason: This is a manuscript sheet of Gauss's well-known decimal-period table for primes below 1000, published in Werke II. It is pure computation with no new idea; it is interesting only as working material (corrections, digit-count checks).

checkable.asserts: period lengths implied by the page
the four 397-periods are those of 139, 225, 150, 10 over 397, with the endings shown (last one 403022670, not 303022670)

checkable.sympy: jacobi_symbol(74,373)==-1 and jacobi_symbol(10,373)==1 and jacobi_symbol(296,401)==-1 and jacobi_symbol(10,401)==1
checkable.asserts: the second period for 373 and 401 is the non-residue coset
the circled 2316 is the total digit count of the page

transcription_corrections: The bottom '(2316)' is the total number of digits on the page, i.e. the sum of p−1.
p=373 line 2: the group transcribed '6273{+458+}5940' should read 6273458445040 (13 digits) to agree with 74/373; '458' is Gauss's insertion.
p=397 second period begins 5667506297 2292191435… (a struck prefix precedes it); the '72292[?]914' group is 7229219[1]4 with irregular grouping.
p=397 fourth period: the last line should be 403022670; its first digit is hidden by the tear, and the pencil '303022670' is wrong.
p=401: the struck group at the start of the first period (before 7381546134) is cancelled. That period is 296/401, ending 1296758104; the second period (10/401) begins 0249376558.
